questions.question: What are the differences between HashMap, TreeMap, and LinkedHashMap?
questions.title: Map Implementations Comparison
questions.direct_answer: `HashMap` provides expected O(1) lookup with no promised iteration order. `LinkedHashMap` adds predictable iteration—normally insertion order, or access order when constructed with `accessOrder=true`—while keeping expected O(1) basic operations. `TreeMap` sorts keys by natural order or a comparator and provides O(log n) lookup and navigation.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of Map implementation trade-offs and when to choose each based on ordering and performance requirements
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Confusing LinkedHashMap's insertion-order preservation with TreeMap's sorted order, or thinking all Maps have the same performance characteristics
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention LinkedHashMap's access-order mode for LRU caches and TreeMap's NavigableMap interface for range queries

sections.title: Three Map Flavors for Different Needs
sections.content:
`HashMap`, `LinkedHashMap`, and `TreeMap` all store key-value mappings, but they make different ordering and performance promises.

- **`HashMap`** has no promised iteration order. With well-distributed stable hashes, basic operations have expected O(1) performance.
- **`LinkedHashMap`** maintains a linked iteration order. Its default is insertion order; the three-argument constructor can select access order for LRU-style policies. Basic operations remain expected O(1), with extra link storage.
- **`TreeMap`** sorts keys using natural ordering or a `Comparator`. Lookup and updates are O(log n), and it offers nearest-key and range-view operations through `NavigableMap`.

The right choice follows the required contract: no order, predictable insertion/access order, or sorted navigation. `HashMap` is a common starting point, not a universal fastest choice.

sections.title: Map Implementations at a Glance
sections.content:
emerald|HashMap|~Hash table, no order|expected O(1) get/put|one null key allowed|the usual unordered default
blue|LinkedHashMap|~HashMap + linked list|expected O(1) get/put|insertion or access order|access-order = LRU cache
violet|TreeMap|~Red-black tree|O(log n) get/put|sorted by key; natural ordering rejects null|NavigableMap range queries
amber|Pick by need|~Order vs speed|no order -> HashMap|remember order -> LinkedHashMap|sorted/ranges -> TreeMap

sections.content:
One question — do you care about order? — picks the class for almost every real case. ```mermaid flowchart TD Q["Need a Map?"] --> O{"Care about order?"} O -->|"No"| H["HashMap
expected O(1), no order"] O -->|"Insertion order"| L["LinkedHashMap
expected O(1), keeps order"] O -->|"Sorted keys"| T["TreeMap
O(log n), sorted"] L --> LRU["access-order mode
powers an LRU cache"] T --> R["NavigableMap
range queries"] ``` Start at the top, and the ordering choice walks you straight to the right class.

rows: Natural ordering rejects null; comparator decides otherwise

sections.title: HashMap when iteration order actually matters
Match the Map to the ordering requirement
When to Choose Each Map
sections.content:
Use **`HashMap`** when you need fast key-value lookups and don't care about iteration order — caching user sessions by sessionId, or storing product prices by SKU.

Use **`LinkedHashMap`** when you need predictable iteration order, like rendering form fields in the order they were added, or when building an **LRU cache** with access-order mode.

Use **`TreeMap`** when you need sorted keys for **range queries** — all orders between two timestamps, or products inside a price range. It's also handy when you want sorted iteration without re-sorting a list every time.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Confusing insertion order with sorted order:** freshers think `LinkedHashMap` sorts entries, but it only preserves the order you put them in — `TreeMap` is the one that sorts.
- **Using TreeMap for simple lookups:** choosing `TreeMap` when you don't need sorting wastes memory and speed — `O(log n)` is slower than `HashMap`'s `expected O(1)` for plain get/put.
- **Forgetting null key restrictions:** natural-order `TreeMap` rejects a null key; a custom comparator decides whether null is supported, while `HashMap` and `LinkedHashMap` allow one null key.
- **Assuming HashMap order is stable:** the order can even change across resizes, so never rely on it for output.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- **HashMap:** no order promise; expected O(1) basic operations.
- **LinkedHashMap:** insertion order by default; optional access order; expected O(1) basics.
- **TreeMap:** sorted keys, O(log n), range and nearest-key operations.
- **Access order:** must be enabled in the constructor; it is not the default.
- **Choice:** specify the order and query operations the application actually needs.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
HashMap is the normal map when I need key lookup and do not need an iteration order; its basic operations are expected O(1) with good hashes. LinkedHashMap adds a linked order. It uses insertion order by default, or access order when explicitly configured, which can support a simple LRU policy. TreeMap keeps keys sorted and provides O(log n) lookup, navigation, and range views.

I choose from the required ordering and query behavior rather than saying one map is always faster. I also account for null rules, comparator consistency, memory overhead, and concurrency separately.

questions.question: How can you implement a simple LRU cache using LinkedHashMap?
questions.title: LRU Cache with LinkedHashMap
questions.direct_answer: For a small, single-threaded bounded LRU map, create a `LinkedHashMap` with `accessOrder=true` and override `removeEldestEntry()` to evict when `size()` exceeds the limit. This demonstrates the policy, but it is not a complete production cache: it is not thread-safe and has no expiry, loading, statistics, or weighted eviction.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of LinkedHashMap's access-order feature and practical application of inheritance to customize collection behavior
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing LinkedHashMap has a three-parameter constructor with accessOrder boolean, or trying to implement LRU from scratch without using this feature
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show the actual concise implementation—it's only a few lines and demonstrates you know this classic Java interview pattern

sections.title: LinkedHashMap's Built-in LRU Support
sections.content:
An **LRU (least recently used) policy** evicts the entry whose most recent qualifying access is oldest when a size limit is exceeded. `LinkedHashMap` can demonstrate this policy with two features.

Construct it with `accessOrder=true` so defined access operations move an entry toward the end of iteration order. Then override `removeEldestEntry()` and return true when `size()` exceeds the chosen limit. The hook is considered after a new mapping is inserted, so the entry at the beginning is removed after capacity is exceeded.

This makes a useful small, single-threaded bounded map. It is not a full production cache: it is not thread-safe, has no time-based expiry, loading, refresh, weighted size, or built-in metrics, and its access-order reads modify iteration order. A cache library is normally better when those features or concurrency are required.

sections.title: LinkedHashMap LRU Recipe at a Glance
sections.content:
blue|Step 1|~Enable access order|super(cap, 0.75f, true)|third arg = accessOrder|default false = FIFO
emerald|Step 2|~Override the hook|removeEldestEntry(e)|return size() > capacity|called after every put
violet|How it reorders|~get/put move to tail|most recent at the end|eldest at the head|head is evicted first
amber|Caveat|~Not thread-safe|wrap synchronizedMap|or use Caffeine/Guava|production needs concurrency

sections.title: How Eviction Works After Every Put
sections.content:
Access-order mode plus the `removeEldestEntry` hook evict the head entry automatically. ```mermaid flowchart TD P["put or get a key"] --> M["entry moves to the tail
most recently used"] M --> C{"size greater than capacity?"} C -->|"No"| K["keep all entries"] C -->|"Yes"| E["removeEldestEntry returns true
evict the head entry"] E --> H["head = least recently used"] ``` The head is always the least recently used entry, so eviction needs no manual tracking.

sections.title: Simple LRU Cache with LinkedHashMap
When to Use LinkedHashMap for LRU
sections.content:
Use this approach for a simple **in-memory cache** with bounded size — caching DB query results keyed by query string, or recently accessed user profiles by userId. It's perfect for **single-threaded** code, or when you control synchronization yourself.

It fits lightweight caching of API responses where you want automatic eviction of old data with no cleanup logic. For production **multi-threaded** caches, reach instead for **Caffeine** or **Guava Cache**, which handle concurrency and richer eviction policies for you.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Forgetting the accessOrder parameter:** the two-arg constructor `new LinkedHashMap(capacity, loadFactor)` gives insertion order, so `get` won't reorder and your LRU silently behaves like FIFO.
- **Not overriding removeEldestEntry:** the default always returns `false`, so nothing is ever evicted.
- **Ignoring thread safety:** concurrent `put` or `get` can corrupt the internal linked list, causing `ConcurrentModificationException` or worse.
- **Misreading 'eldest':** the eldest entry is the head of the access order (least recently accessed), not the one with the oldest value.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- **Access order:** construct `LinkedHashMap` with the third argument `true`.
- **Eldest entry:** first entry in access order—the least recently accessed under that policy.
- **Eviction hook:** override `removeEldestEntry` and evict when size exceeds the limit.
- **Scope:** good for a small single-threaded bounded map.
- **Not a full cache:** no concurrency, expiry, loading, weighting, refresh, or metrics.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
A simple LRU policy can use LinkedHashMap in access-order mode. I call the three-argument constructor with `true`, then override `removeEldestEntry` to return true when the size exceeds the limit. Defined access operations move an entry to the end, so the first entry is the least recently used and is evicted after a new mapping pushes the map over capacity.

I describe this as a small single-threaded bounded map, not a complete cache. It needs external coordination for concurrency and does not provide expiry, loading, weighted eviction, or statistics. For production caching I would normally use a cache library when those requirements exist.

speakable_v2.hook: LinkedHashMap has a built-in LRU mode. One constructor flag and one overridden method give you a cache in about ten lines.

beats.text: An LRU cache drops the least recently used entry when it's full. LRU just means least recently used. LinkedHashMap supports this through its `accessOrder` flag. Turn it on, and every get or put moves the touched entry to the end. The least recently used entry stays at the head.

Java's designers planned for this pattern. The `removeEldestEntry` method exists as an extension point, built for exactly this case. It's a protected hook you override, so you skip writing the eviction logic yourself.

items: The constructor `super(capacity, 0.75f, true)` flips on access-order mode with its third argument.
The `removeEldestEntry` override returns size greater than capacity, so the head entry leaves when the map fills up.
Every get and put moves the touched entry to the tail. The most recent one sits at the back.
This map isn't thread-safe. A concurrent use needs a wrapper like `Collections.synchronizedMap`.

beats.text: Picture a cache with capacity three. Add user one, user two, user three. Now read user one, and it jumps to the back. Add user four, and the cache drops user two. Here's the non-obvious part. Without access-order mode, get won't reorder anything. You'd evict the oldest inserted entry instead. That's FIFO, not LRU.

items: Skip the access-order flag and you get FIFO, not LRU. The default constructor keeps insertion order.
The cache isn't thread-safe on its own. Concurrent reads and writes can corrupt the internal list.

speakable_v2.cap: So an LRU cache is three small steps. Extend LinkedHashMap, pass access-order true, and override removeEldestEntry.

questions.question: What are the NavigableMap methods in TreeMap and when are they useful?
questions.title: TreeMap NavigableMap Methods
questions.direct_answer: `NavigableMap` adds nearest-key operations such as `floorKey`, `ceilingKey`, `lowerKey`, and `higherKey`, plus bounded views such as `headMap`, `tailMap`, and `subMap`. TreeMap finds boundary keys in O(log n); creating a range view is efficient, but reading k entries from that view still takes O(k) after reaching the start. The views are backed by the map and enforce their bounds.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of TreeMap's sorted capabilities beyond basic put/get operations and knowledge of NavigableMap interface methods
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using TreeMap only for sorted iteration without realizing it provides powerful range query operations that would be expensive with other Maps
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Provide a concrete real-world example like finding events in a time range or stock prices closest to a target value

sections.title: NavigableMap: Beyond Simple Sorted Iteration
sections.content:
`TreeMap` keeps keys sorted, and its `NavigableMap` API uses that order for nearby-key and range operations.

`floorKey(k)` returns the greatest key less than or equal to `k`; `ceilingKey(k)` returns the least key greater than or equal to it. `lowerKey` and `higherKey` are strict. Entry-returning forms such as `floorEntry` provide both key and value.

`headMap`, `tailMap`, and `subMap` return **backed range views**, not copied maps. Changes flow between the view and the original map, and inserting a key outside a view's range fails. Overloads let the caller choose inclusive or exclusive endpoints; the simpler `subMap(from, to)` is inclusive at the lower bound and exclusive at the upper bound.

TreeMap can locate a boundary in O(log n). Creating the view does not traverse every entry, but processing k entries in it still costs O(k) after navigation to the starting point.

sections.title: NavigableMap Methods at a Glance
sections.content:
blue|Nearest (inclusive)|~floor and ceiling|floorKey(k): largest <= k|ceilingKey(k): smallest >= k|null if none qualifies
emerald|Nearest (strict)|~higher and lower|lowerKey(k): largest < k|higherKey(k): smallest > k|excludes equality
violet|Range views|~live, backed views|headMap(k): keys < k|tailMap(k): keys >= k|subMap(from, to): [from, to)
amber|Reverse|~descending order|descendingMap()|descendingKeySet()|no manual sort needed

sections.title: From a Target Key to a Result
sections.content:
Hand `NavigableMap` a target key, and it returns a nearby key or a range slice — always in `O(log n)`. ```mermaid flowchart TD T["target key k"] --> N{"what do you need?"} N -->|"key at or below"| F["floorKey(k)"] N -->|"key at or above"| C["ceilingKey(k)"] N -->|"a range"| S["subMap(from, to)
headMap / tailMap"] F --> O["O(log n) on the red-black tree"] C --> O S --> O ``` Every path stays `O(log n)` because the tree is already sorted.

sections.title: Using NavigableMap for Event Scheduling
When NavigableMap Shines
sections.content:
Use **`floorKey()`/`ceilingKey()`** for the closest match to a target — the stock price at or before a timestamp, or the nearest free appointment slot.

Use **`subMap()`** for **range queries** like all orders between two dates, products in a price band, or log entries inside a time window.

Use **`headMap()`/`tailMap()`** for everything before or after a threshold — events before a deadline, scores above a cutoff. All of these are `O(log n)` versus `O(n)` for filtering a list. A leaderboard can store scores as keys and call `descendingMap()` to walk from highest to lowest.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Iterating to find the nearest key:** looping to find the closest key is `O(n)`; `floorKey()` or `ceilingKey()` does it in `O(log n)` and is the whole reason to use `TreeMap`.
- **Confusing floor/ceiling with higher/lower:** `floorKey` is less-than-or-equal, `lowerKey` is strictly-less-than — mixing them gives off-by-one range boundaries.
- **Modifying range views wrongly:** `subMap()` is a live view; putting an out-of-range key into it throws `IllegalArgumentException`, which surprises freshers expecting a copy.
- **Forgetting descending views:** `descendingMap()` and `descendingKeySet()` give reverse iteration with no manual sorting.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- **Nearest keys:** `floor`/`ceiling` include equality; `lower`/`higher` are strict.
- **Key or entry:** choose `floorKey` versus `floorEntry` and similar pairs.
- **Range views:** `headMap`, `tailMap`, and `subMap` are backed by the original map.
- **Bounds:** overloads control inclusivity; out-of-range inserts through a view fail.
- **Cost:** boundary lookup O(log n), then O(k) to visit k returned entries.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
NavigableMap adds operations that use sorted keys. Floor and ceiling find the nearest key at or below or at or above a target, while lower and higher are strict. HeadMap, tailMap, and subMap create bounded views backed by the original map, with overloads for inclusive or exclusive endpoints.

TreeMap locates a boundary in logarithmic time. A range view is cheap to create, but iterating k mappings still takes O(k) after locating the start. Because the view is live, changes affect the original map, and the view rejects keys outside its bounds.

questions.question: What are the modern Map methods — getOrDefault(), computeIfAbsent(), and merge()?
questions.title: Modern Map Methods
questions.direct_answer: `getOrDefault` returns the mapped value, or a fallback only when no mapping exists. `computeIfAbsent` computes when a key is absent or currently maps to null, and stores a non-null result. `merge` inserts a value for an absent or null-mapped key, otherwise combines old and new values; a null remapping result removes the mapping. Atomicity depends on the Map implementation.

interviewer_intent.testing: Knowledge of Java 8+ Map API enhancements that make common patterns more concise and expressive
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using verbose patterns like checking containsKey() then putting, or getting then null-checking then putting, when these methods do it in one atomic operation
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show the frequency counting pattern with merge() using Integer::sum—it's much cleaner than the old get-increment-put approach

sections.title: Modern Map Methods That Replace Boilerplate
sections.content:
These `Map` methods remove common check-then-update boilerplate, but their null and concurrency rules matter.

- **`getOrDefault(key, fallback)`** returns the existing mapped value. If the key is explicitly mapped to `null`, it returns `null`, not the fallback.
- **`computeIfAbsent(key, function)`** calls the function when the key has no mapping or maps to `null`. A non-null result is stored; a null result leaves no new mapping.
- **`merge(key, value, function)`** uses the supplied non-null value when the key is absent or maps to `null`. Otherwise it combines the old and new values. If the remapping function returns `null`, the mapping is removed.

The default `Map` contracts do not promise synchronization or atomic compound behavior. Concurrent implementations such as `ConcurrentHashMap` strengthen particular methods, but their mapping functions must follow the implementation's restrictions and should stay short and side-effect controlled.

sections.title: Modern Map Methods at a Glance
sections.content:
emerald|getOrDefault|~Safe read|return value or fallback|no null check needed|fallback is eager, keep it cheap
blue|computeIfAbsent|~Lazy get-or-create|runs fn only if absent|stores + returns value|grouping: Map<K,List<V>>
violet|merge|~Insert or combine|absent -> store value|present -> fn(old, new)|counting: merge(k, 1, Integer::sum)
amber|compute|~General update|v is null if absent|handle insert + update|return null removes the key

sections.title: One Intent, One Method
sections.content:
Name what you need, and the method picks itself. ```mermaid flowchart TD N{"what do you need?"} -->|"safe read"| G["getOrDefault
value or fallback"] N -->|"get or create"| C["computeIfAbsent
build only if absent"] N -->|"insert or combine"| M["merge
old + new via function"] M --> F["frequency counting
merge(k, 1, Integer::sum)"] ``` Each modern method maps to a single, clear intent.

sections.title: Practical Uses of Modern Map Methods
When to Use Each Method
sections.content:
Use **`getOrDefault()`** for reading config or cache data that might be missing — you want a sensible fallback, not a null check.

Use **`computeIfAbsent()`** for nested structures like grouping (`Map` of `List`) or caching expensive results — you pay the cost of creating the value only when the key is missing.

Use **`merge()`** for aggregations: frequency counting, summing by category, or combining maps where both new keys and updates matter. The remap function takes old and new, so `Integer::sum` counts, `String::concat` appends, and a lambda handles custom merges.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Manual get-then-null-check-then-put:** writing `if (map.get(key) == null) map.put(key, new ArrayList<>());` instead of `computeIfAbsent(key, k -> new ArrayList<>())`.
- **Eager defaults in getOrDefault():** `getOrDefault(key, expensive())` always runs `expensive()` even when the key exists — use `computeIfAbsent()` for lazy work.
- **Skipping merge for counting:** `put(id, getOrDefault(id, 0) + 1)` is noisier than `merge(id, 1, Integer::sum)`.
- **Confusing computeIfAbsent with putIfAbsent:** `putIfAbsent` stores a pre-computed value, while `computeIfAbsent` computes it lazily only when needed.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- **getOrDefault:** fallback only when no mapping exists; a mapped null is still a mapping.
- **computeIfAbsent:** compute for absent or null-mapped key; store only a non-null result.
- **merge:** insert for absent/null, combine for non-null existing value, remove if remapping returns null.
- **Useful examples:** group values with `computeIfAbsent`; count with `merge`.
- **Concurrency:** atomicity and callback rules come from the concrete Map implementation.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
`getOrDefault` returns a fallback only when the key has no mapping; if a HashMap key is present with a null value, the result is null. `computeIfAbsent` runs its function for an absent or null-mapped key and stores the result only when it is non-null. It is useful for creating a list on first use. `merge` stores the supplied value for an absent or null-mapped key, otherwise combines it with the old value; returning null from the remapping function removes the mapping.

These methods make intent clearer, but I do not promise one lookup or atomicity for every Map. A concurrent map may provide stronger atomic behavior for a method, subject to its documented callback restrictions.
